'''Francis Gordon Albert Stone''' [[Order of the British Empire|CBE]], [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]], [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry|FRSC]] (19 May 1925&nbsp;– 6 April 2011), always known as Gordon, was a British [[inorganic chemistry|chemist]] who was a prolific and decorated scholar. He specialized in the synthesis of [[main group]] and [[transition metal]] [[organometallic]] compounds. He was the author of more than 900 academic publications resulting in an [[h-index]] of 72 in 2011.<ref>{{Cite web |title=RSC images |url=https://www.rsc.org/images/H-index%20ranking%20of%20living%20chemists(March%202011)_tcm18-85867.pdf}}</ref>

==Early life==
Gordon Stone was born in Exeter, Devon in 1925, the only child of Sidney Charles Stone, a [[Civil Service (United Kingdom)|civil servant]], and Florence Beatrice Stone (née Coles).<ref name=Uni>Bristol University Obituary, [http://www.bristol.ac.uk/news/2011/7593.html F Gordon A Stone], retrieved 08/03/2012</ref>  He received his B.A. in 1948 and Ph.D. in 1951, both from [[Christ's College, Cambridge]] ([[Cambridge University]]), England, where he studied under [[Harry Julius Emeléus]].

==Academic life==
After graduating from Cambridge, he was a [[Fulbright Scholar]] at the [[University of Southern California]] for two years, before being appointed as an instructor in the Chemistry Department at [[Harvard University]], and was appointed [[assistant professor]] in 1957.<ref name=Uni/> He was the [[Robert A. Welch Foundation|Robert A. Welch Distinguished Professor of Chemistry]] at [[Baylor University]], [[Texas]] until 2010, but his most productive period was as Professor of Inorganic Chemistry at [[Bristol University]], England (1963–1990), where he published hundreds of papers over the course of 27 years.  In research he competed with his contemporary [[Geoffrey Wilkinson]].

Elected to the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] in 1970, and to the [[Royal Society]] in 1976, he was awarded the [[Davy Medal]] "In recognition of his many distinguished contributions to organometallic chemistry, including the discovery that species containing carbon-metal of metal-metal multiple bonds are versatile reagents for synthesis of cluster compounds with bonds between different transition elements" in 1989.<ref>{{cite book |last=Barker |first=Philip |year=1999 |title=Top 1000 Scientists |page=321 |publisher=Lewes Book Guild |isbn=1857764056 }}</ref>

Among the many foci of his studies were complexes of [[fluorocarbon]], [[isocyanide]], [[polyolefin]], [[alkylidene]] and alkylidyne ligands.  At Baylor, he maintained a research program on [[boron hydrides]], a lifelong interest.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Stone | first1 = F. G. A. | last2 = Emeléus | first2 = H. J. | title = Reaction of diborane with some alkene oxides and vinyl compounds | journal = Journal of the Chemical Society | volume = 1950 | pages = 2755–9 | doi = 10.1039/JR9500002755 }}</ref>

In 1988 he chaired the Review Committee commissioned by the British Government (the now-dissolved [[University Grants Committee (UK)|University Grants Committee]]) to carry out a review of chemistry in UK academia ("University Chemistry&nbsp;— The Way Forward", "The Stone Report").<ref name=THE>Times Higher Education, [http://www.timeshighereducation.co.uk/story.asp?storycode=415940 Obituary], retrieved 07/04/2012</ref><ref name=Report/> His main recommendation, "that the UGC <nowiki> [...] </nowiki> fund properly not fewer than 30 chemistry departments" and that "at least 20 of these departments have 30 or more academic staff <nowiki> [...] </nowiki>to compete successfully at the international level"<ref name=Report>University Chemistry&nbsp;— The Way Forward, The Report of the Chemistry Review, University Grants Committee, Her Majesty's Stationery Office, published 1988, {{ISBN|0117012122}}</ref> was never implemented.<ref name=THE/>

His autobiography ''Leaving No Stone Unturned, Pathways in Organometallic Chemistry'', was published in 1993.<ref name=auto>Leaving No Stone Unturned, Pathways in Organometallic Chemistry, F. Gordon A. Stone, Profiles, Pathways, and Dreams, Series Editor Jeffrey I. Seeman, [[American Chemical Society]], {{ISBN|0841218269}}</ref> With Wilkinson, he edited the influential series ''Comprehensive Organometallic Chemistry''.  With [[Robert West (chemist)|Robert West]], he edited the series ''Advances in Organometallic Chemistry''.

The Gordon Stone Lecture series at the University of Bristol is named in his honour.<ref>[[University of Bristol]], Inorganic and Materials Chemistry, http://www.inchm.bris.ac.uk/events_past.htm#stone, retrieved 25/03/2012</ref>

Annual Stone Symposiums are also held at Baylor University in his honor.

==Awards==
* [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry]] (1970)
* [[Royal Society#Fellows|Fellow of the Royal Society]] (1976),<ref name ="bristol uni">[http://www.bris.ac.uk/news/2011/7593.html F Gordon A Stone, 1925-2011], retrieved 25 October 2012</ref> Vice-President 1987-1988
* Chugaev Medal of the Kurnakov Institute ([[Russian Academy of Sciences]]) (1978)
* [[Royal Society of Chemistry]]’s [[Ludwig Mond Award]] (1983)
* [[American Chemical Society]]’s award in Inorganic Chemistry (1985)
* Royal Society of Chemistry’s Sir Edward Frankland Prize Lectureship (1988)
* [[Royal Society]]'s [[Davy Medal]] (1989)
* Royal Society of Chemistry’s [[Longstaff Prize]] (1990)
* [[Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (1990)

==Personal life==
He married Judith Hislop (1928-2008) of Sydney, Australia in 1956 with whom he had three sons.
